prompt:
Shown is a segment of length 19, marked with 20 points dividing the segment into 19 segments of length 1. Draw 20 semicircular arcs, each of whose endpoints are two of the 20 marked points, satisfying all of the following conditions:

1. When the drawing is complete, there will be:
   * 8 arcs with diameter 1,
   * 6 arcs with diameter 3,
   * 4 arcs with diameter 5,
   * 2 arcs with diameter 7.
2. Each marked point is the endpoint of exactly two arcs: one above the segment and one below the segment.
3. No two distinct arcs can intersect except at their endpoints.
4. No two distinct arcs can connect the same pair of points. (That is, there can be no full circles.)

Three arcs have already been drawn for you, as shown in the picture.

There is a unique solution, but you do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible. You merely need to find an answer that satisfies the conditions of the problem.

solutions.title: Build the arcs from the constraints
solutions.body:
Number the points $1, 2, \dots, 20$ from left to right. The given arcs are $6$–$11$ (above, diameter 5) and $8$–$9$, $13$–$14$ (below, diameter 1).

**Useful facts.**
* Every diameter is odd, so every arc joins an odd-numbered point to an even-numbered point.
* The 10 arcs above form a non-crossing matching of all 20 points, and so do the 10 arcs below. In a non-crossing matching, the points strictly inside an arc must be matched among themselves.
* Point 1 must be joined (above and below) to two *different* points among $2, 4, 6, 8$; likewise point 20 to two different points among $19, 17, 15, 13$.

**Above.** Inside the arc $6$–$11$ are points $7, 8, 9, 10$, which must be matched among themselves without crossing; diameter 3 for $7$–$10$ would force $8$–$9$ above as well, a full circle with the given arc $8$–$9$ below. So above we have $7$–$8$ and $9$–$10$. Points $1$–$5$ lie to the left of the big arc; an odd number of them must be joined over the arc $6$–$11$ to points $\ge 12$, which needs diameter $\ge 7$, so exactly $5$–$12$ (diameter 7) is drawn above. Points $1$–$4$ are then matched among themselves above ($1$–$2$, $3$–$4$ or $1$–$4$, $2$–$3$), and points $13$–$20$ among themselves.

**Finishing.** Only a handful of combinations remain for the left block ($1$–$6$ below) and the right block ($11$–$20$). Checking them against the required numbers of arcs of each diameter (only one more diameter-7 arc is allowed, and it must be on the right) and against the no-full-circle rule leaves exactly one possibility.

**Final drawing.**
* Above: $1$–$4$, $2$–$3$, $5$–$12$, $6$–$11$, $7$–$8$, $9$–$10$, $13$–$20$, $14$–$19$, $15$–$18$, $16$–$17$.
* Below: $1$–$6$, $2$–$5$, $3$–$4$, $7$–$10$, $8$–$9$, $11$–$16$, $12$–$15$, $13$–$14$, $17$–$20$, $18$–$19$.

**Check.** Diameters: 1 occurs for $2$–$3$, $7$–$8$, $9$–$10$, $16$–$17$, $3$–$4$, $8$–$9$, $13$–$14$, $18$–$19$ (8 arcs); 3 for $1$–$4$, $15$–$18$, $2$–$5$, $7$–$10$, $12$–$15$, $17$–$20$ (6 arcs); 5 for $6$–$11$, $14$–$19$, $1$–$6$, $11$–$16$ (4 arcs); 7 for $5$–$12$, $13$–$20$ (2 arcs). Each side is a nested (non-crossing) perfect matching, every point has one arc above and one below, and no pair appears on both sides. A computer search over all non-crossing matchings confirms that this is the only solution.

**Answer: the arcs listed above.**

prompt: Given a sphere, a *great circle* of the sphere is a circle on the sphere whose diameter is also a diameter of the sphere. For a given positive integer $n$, the surface of a sphere is divided into several regions by $n$ great circles, and each region is colored black or white. We say that a coloring is *good* if any two adjacent regions (that share an arc as boundary, not just a finite number of points) have different colors. Find, with proof, all positive integers $n$ such that in every good coloring with $n$ great circles, the sum of the areas of the black regions is equal to the sum of the areas of the white regions.
answer: Exactly the **odd** $n$. (For odd $n$ antipodal points always have opposite colors; for even $n$ take all circles through two poles with unequal alternating lune angles.)

solutions.title: Antipodal points
solutions.body:
**Odd $n$ works.** Let $P$ be any point not on the $n$ circles, and let $Q$ be its antipode. Choose a great circle $C$ through $P$ and $Q$ that avoids the finitely many points where two of the given circles meet. Each given great circle meets $C$ in two antipodal points, so exactly one of them lies on the open half of $C$ from $P$ to $Q$. Walking along that half from $P$ to $Q$, we therefore cross the given circles exactly $n$ times, each time through the interior of an arc, i.e. passing into an adjacent region. In a good coloring the color changes at every crossing, so after $n$ (odd) changes the color of $Q$ is opposite to that of $P$.

Hence the antipodal map $X \mapsto -X$ sends the black part of the sphere onto the white part (up to the circles themselves, which have zero area). Since this map preserves area, black and white areas are equal.

**Even $n$ fails.** Let all $n$ great circles pass through the north and south poles $N$, $S$. They cut the sphere into $2n$ lunes; adjacent lunes must have different colors, so the colors alternate around the axis. Choose the half-meridians bounding the lunes so that the lune angles, going around, are $a, b, a, b, \dots$ with $a \ne b$ and $n(a + b) = 2\pi$. Because $n$ is even, any $n$ consecutive angles add up to $\tfrac n2(a+b) = \pi$, so the half-meridian at each boundary and the one $n$ steps further are antipodal and together form a great circle — we really have $n$ great circles. The lunes of angle $a$ all get one color, and its area fraction is $\frac{na}{2\pi} \ne \frac12$.

For example, with $n = 2$ and the two circles at $30^\circ$ to each other, one color covers $\frac16$ of the sphere and the other $\frac56$.

**Answer: all odd positive integers $n$.** ∎

prompt:
Prove that there is a unique 1000-digit number $N$ in base 2022 with the following properties:

1. All of the digits of $N$ (in base 2022) are 1's or 2's, and
2. $N$ is a multiple of the base-10 number $2^{1000}$.

(Note that you must prove both that such a number exists and that there is not more than one such number. You do not have to write down the number! In fact, please don't!)
answer: Proof. Since $2022 = 2\cdot 1011$, two different digit strings of 1's and 2's whose lowest differing digit is in position $j$ differ by $2^j\cdot(\text{odd})$; so the $2^{1000}$ numbers have distinct residues mod $2^{1000}$ and exactly one is $\equiv 0$. (Equivalently: build $N$ digit by digit by induction.)

solutions.title: Induction on the number of digits
solutions.body:
We prove more generally: for every $k \ge 1$ there is exactly one $k$-digit base-2022 number with all digits in $\{1, 2\}$ that is divisible by $2^k$. For $k = 1$: $2$ is divisible by $2$ and $1$ is not.

Suppose the claim holds for $k - 1$, with unique number $M = m\cdot 2^{k-1}$. Put a digit $d \in \{1, 2\}$ in front:
$$N = d\cdot 2022^{k-1} + M = 2^{k-1}\left(d\cdot 1011^{k-1} + m\right).$$
Since $1011^{k-1}$ is odd, $d\cdot 1011^{k-1} + m$ is even for exactly one choice of $d$ ($d = 1$ if $m$ is odd, $d = 2$ if $m$ is even). So exactly one extension of $M$ is divisible by $2^k$: existence.

Uniqueness: if $N$ is any $k$-digit number of 1's and 2's divisible by $2^k$, with leading digit $d$, then $N' = N - d\cdot 2022^{k-1} = N - 2^{k-1}d\cdot 1011^{k-1}$ is a $(k-1)$-digit number of 1's and 2's divisible by $2^{k-1}$, so $N' = M$ by the induction hypothesis, and then $d$ is forced as shown. Taking $k = 1000$ proves the statement. ∎

solutions.title: Counting residues
solutions.body:
There are exactly $2^{1000}$ numbers $N = \sum_{i=0}^{999} d_i\, 2022^i$ with all $d_i \in \{1, 2\}$, and exactly $2^{1000}$ residues modulo $2^{1000}$. We show that two different such numbers are never congruent mod $2^{1000}$; then they hit every residue exactly once, in particular $0$ exactly once — which is the claim.

Take $N \ne N'$ and let $j$ be the lowest position where their digits differ (so $d_j - d'_j = \pm 1$). Then
$$N - N' = \pm 2022^j + \sum_{i > j}(d_i - d'_i)\,2022^i = 2^j\left(\pm 1011^j + 2\cdot(\text{integer})\right),$$
because $2022^i = 2^i\cdot 1011^i$ is divisible by $2^{j+1}$ for $i > j$. The bracket is odd, so $N - N'$ is divisible by $2^j$ but not by $2^{j+1}$; as $j \le 999$, it is not divisible by $2^{1000}$. ∎

prompt: Grogg and Winnie are playing a game using a deck of 50 cards numbered 1 through 50. They take turns with Grogg going first. On each turn a player chooses a card from the deck—this choice is made deliberately, not at random—and then adds it to one of two piles (both piles are empty at the start of the game). After all 50 cards are in the two piles, the values of the cards in each pile are summed, and Winnie wins the positive difference of the sums of the two piles, in dollars. (For instance, if the first pile has cards summing to 510 and the second pile has cards summing to 765, then Winnie wins \$255.) Winnie wants to win as much as possible, and Grogg wants Winnie to win as little as possible. If they both play with perfect strategy, find (with proof) the amount that Winnie wins.

solutions.title: Strategies for both players
solutions.body:
Call the current difference of the two pile sums the *score*.

**Winnie can guarantee at least \$75.** She pairs the cards as $\{49, 50\}$ and $\{2k - 1, 2k\}$ for $k = 1, \dots, 24$. Grogg always moves first in a fresh pair (Winnie only ever completes the pair Grogg just opened), so she can always answer immediately:
* when Grogg plays 49 or 50, she plays the other one **on the same pile**;
* when Grogg plays $2k-1$ or $2k$, she plays the other one **on the other pile**.

In the end, 49 and 50 contribute $99$ to one side, and each of the 24 small pairs contributes $\pm 1$ to the difference. So the final score is at least $99 - 24 = 75$.

**Grogg can hold Winnie to at most \$75.** On each of his turns Grogg plays the largest remaining card on the pile with the smaller sum (either pile if they are equal). Let $s_i$ be the score before Grogg's $i$-th turn ($s_1 = 0$) and $m_i$ the card he plays then.

* $m_i \le 51 - i$: by induction, before Grogg's $i$-th turn all cards larger than $51 - i$ are gone; he removes the largest remaining card, so afterwards all cards larger than $50 - i$ are gone.
* $s_{i+1} \le \max(s_i - 1,\ 2m_i - 1)$: every card Winnie can then play is smaller than $m_i$. If $s_i \ge m_i$, Grogg's card lowers the score to $s_i - m_i$ and Winnie's card $c \le m_i - 1$ raises it to at most $s_i - 1$. If $s_i < m_i$, the score after Grogg's move is $m_i - s_i \le m_i$, and after Winnie's at most $m_i + (m_i - 1) = 2m_i - 1$.

Hence $s_2 \le 99$, and if $s_i \le 101 - i$ then $s_{i+1} \le \max(100 - i,\ 101 - 2i) = 100 - i$. By induction the final score is $s_{26} \le 75$.

**Conclusion.** With perfect play Winnie wins exactly \$75. (For instance, with these strategies the piles can end as $\{1, 3, 5, \dots, 49, 50\}$ with sum 675 and $\{2, 4, \dots, 48\}$ with sum 600.)

**Answer: \$75**

solutions.title: Check on small decks
solutions.body:
The same two strategies work for a deck $1, \dots, 2m$: Winnie pairs $\{2m - 1, 2m\}$ on one pile and $m - 1$ small pairs on opposite piles, getting at least $(4m - 1) - (m - 1) = 3m$; Grogg's greedy strategy gives at most $3m$. A full game-tree search (minimax) for decks of $2, 4, \dots, 14$ cards gives values $3, 6, 9, \dots, 21$, i.e. exactly $3m$, confirming the pattern. For $50$ cards, $m = 25$ and the value is $3\cdot 25 = 75$.

**Answer: \$75**

prompt:
We call a positive integer $n$ *sixish* if $n = p(p+6)$, where $p$ and $p+6$ are prime numbers. For example, $187 = 11\cdot 17$ is sixish, but $475 = 19\cdot 25$ is not sixish.

Define a function $f$ on positive integers such that $f(n)$ is the sum of the squares of the positive divisors of $n$. For example, $f(10) = 1^2 + 2^2 + 5^2 + 10^2 = 130$.

(a) Find, with proof, an irreducible polynomial function $g(x)$ with integer coefficients such that $f(n) = g(n)$ for all sixish $n$. ("Irreducible" means that $g(x)$ cannot be factored as the product of two polynomials of smaller degree with integer coefficients.)

(b) We call a positive integer $n$ *pseudo-sixish* if $n$ is not sixish but nonetheless $f(n) = g(n)$, where $g(n)$ is the polynomial function that you found in part (a). Find, with proof, all pseudo-sixish positive integers.
answer: (a) $g(x) = x^2 + 2x + 37$. (b) The only pseudo-sixish number is $27$.

solutions.title: Pair up the divisors
solutions.body:
**(a)** If $n = p(p+6)$ with both factors prime, the divisors are $1, p, p+6, n$, so
$$f(n) = 1 + p^2 + (p+6)^2 + n^2 = n^2 + 2p(p+6) + 37 = n^2 + 2n + 37.$$
Take $g(x) = x^2 + 2x + 37$. Its discriminant $4 - 148 < 0$, so it has no rational roots and, being quadratic, is irreducible over the integers.

**(b)** We need all $n$ with $f(n) = n^2 + 2n + 37$, i.e.
$$\sum_{d \mid n,\ 1 < d < n} d^2 = 2n + 36. \qquad (*)$$
Pair each proper divisor $d$ with $n/d$. For a pair $d < n/d$:
$$d^2 + (n/d)^2 = (n/d - d)^2 + 2n \ge 2n + 1.$$

* $n = 1$: the left side of $(*)$ is $0 \ne 38$. $n$ prime: left side $0 \ne 2n + 36$.
* $n = p^2$: left side $p^2$, and $p^2 = 2p^2 + 36$ is impossible.
* **Exactly four divisors** ($n = pq$ with primes $p < q$, or $n = p^3$): one pair $r < s$ with $rs = n$, and $(*)$ becomes $(s - r)^2 + 2n = 2n + 36$, so $s - r = 6$. For $n = pq$ this is $q = p + 6$ — sixish, excluded. For $n = p^3$ it is $p^2 - p = 6$, so $p = 3$ and $n = 27$. Indeed $f(27) = 1 + 9 + 81 + 729 = 820 = 27^2 + 54 + 37$. ✓
* **Five divisors** ($n = p^4$): $p^2 + p^4 + p^6 = 2p^4 + 36$, i.e. $p^6 - p^4 + p^2 = 36$; for $p = 2$ the left side is $52$, and it is increasing in $p$. No solution.
* **At least six divisors**: there are at least two pairs, so the left side of $(*)$ is at least $2(2n + 1) = 4n + 2$, which exceeds $2n + 36$ once $n \ge 17$. The numbers below 17 with at least six divisors are $12$ (left side $4+9+16+36 = 65 \ne 60$). No solution.

Hence the only pseudo-sixish number is $27$. ∎

solutions.title: Official approach: $x_n = 36 - (s-r)^2$
solutions.body:
Let $h(n) = g(n) - f(n)$. One checks $h(1) = 39$, $h(p) = 2p + 36$ and $h(p^2) = p^2 + 36$, so pseudo-sixish numbers are not $1$, primes or prime squares. Otherwise write $n = rs$ with $1 < r < s$ (e.g. $r$ the smallest prime factor) and let $x_n$ be the sum of the squares of the divisors other than $1, r, s, n$. Then
$$0 = h(n) = 2rs + 36 - r^2 - s^2 - x_n \iff x_n = 36 - (s - r)^2.$$
If $x_n = 0$, the only divisors are $1, r, s, n$, so $n = pq$ (sixish when $s - r = 6$) or $n = r^3$ with $r^2 - r = 6$, i.e. $n = 27$. If $x_n > 0$ then $x_n \in \{11, 20, 27, 32, 35\}$ must be a sum of distinct squares of divisors larger than 1; only $20 = 2^2 + 4^2$ works, forcing the divisors $1, 2, 4, r, s, n$ — six divisors, so $n = 4q$ or $n = 32$, and neither fits $n = rs$ with the extra divisors exactly $2, 4$. So $27$ is the only one.

A computer check of all $n \le 10^6$ confirms: the solutions of $f(n) = n^2 + 2n + 37$ are $27$ and the sixish numbers $55, 91, 187, \dots$.

**Answer: (a) $g(x) = x^2 + 2x + 37$; (b) only $27$.** ∎
